name: How Japanese players get overseas: agents explained
summary: A beginner's guide to the people and rules behind a Japanese footballer's move abroad: what an agent does, who pays, which doors lead to Europe, and what can go wrong.

cells: The person who finds clubs for a player and negotiates the contract. Needs a FIFA licence since October 2023.
A company that handles a player's ads, TV and daily support. Often a different company from the agent. Example: Hidetoshi Nakata's PR company, Sunny Side Up.
Money the buying club pays the selling club. It is only paid if the player is still under contract.
A player leaves when the contract ends, so the old club gets no fee.
Small payments that go back to the clubs and schools that trained a player. Solidarity is 5% of an international fee, shared across the ages 12 to 23.
A first overseas club that is known for welcoming Japanese players, so the next step up is easier.

sections.title: The story: how Japanese players went overseas

parts.heading: 1. One man and a friendship (1977)
parts.text: The first was Yasuhiko Okudera. There was no agent. Japan's national team held a camp in Germany, Okudera trained with 1. FC Köln, and the Japan coach was a friend of Köln's coach. That friendship was the whole 'transfer system'. For the next twenty years almost nobody followed.

parts.heading: 2. Stars and sponsors (1994–2001)
parts.text: Kazuyoshi Miura went to Italy in 1994 and Hidetoshi Nakata in 1998. Nakata succeeded, and Italy noticed Japan. Japan's first licensed agents appeared around 1999, and in 2001 Junichi Inamoto joined Arsenal. Many in Europe still asked whether these signings were for football or for selling shirts in Asia.

parts.heading: 3. Someone to vouch for them (2003–2010)
parts.text: Thomas Kroth, a German agent who had once played alongside Okudera, began telling German clubs which Japanese players were worth it. Clubs trusted him because he was one of them. Takahara went to Hamburg, Hasebe to Wolfsburg, where he won the league in 2009. In the Netherlands, a club chairman who did business with Japan asked a Dutch coach in Nagoya for a talent and got Keisuke Honda.

parts.heading: 4. The rule that opened the gate (2009)
parts.text: Until 2009 a Japanese club could demand a fee even after a player's contract had ended. The players' association fought that rule and it was scrapped. Suddenly a player at the end of his contract could walk to Europe for free. Japanese clubs lost money. Japanese players gained freedom.

parts.heading: 5. The bargain everyone saw (2010)
parts.text: Borussia Dortmund paid about €350,000 for Shinji Kagawa. He was one of the best players in Germany within months, and two years later Manchester United paid many times that. After Kagawa, 'Japanese player' meant 'cheap and good' to every sporting director in Europe. Uchida, Okazaki, Nagatomo and Yoshida all moved in these years.

parts.heading: 6. Building the bridge on purpose (2017)
parts.text: A Japanese company bought Sint-Truiden, a club in Belgium, and used it as a first step for Japanese players. Tomiyasu, Endo and Kamada each stayed about a season and moved up. What Venlo had done by accident, Sint-Truiden did as a plan.

parts.heading: 7. A normal career path (2020s)
parts.text: Now more than 100 Japanese players are at European clubs. European scouts watch Japanese under-15s. Some players skip the J.League and go to Europe straight from high school. In 2025 a defender moved directly from Kawasaki to Tottenham for about €5.8 million. In 2026 there were a record ten Japanese players at Premier League clubs. Going abroad is no longer a dream for a few; it is the expected next step.

sections.title: What pulls them to Europe: the main trends

cells: A news agency summed up Europe's view in 2026 as 'high quality, low risk'. The head of Sint-Truiden said a Brazilian of the same level costs about three times as much as a Japanese player.
Each success made the next signing easier: Hasebe, Kagawa, then Endo, Mitoma, Kubo. Clubs now believe Japanese players adapt.
European football has become more about passing and pressing, which suits technically precise players. Agent Thomas Kroth adds discipline and self-care.
Clubs can watch every J.League match from an office. Belgian clubs watch the J.League most on the scouting platform Wyscout; Danish and German second-division clubs are rising.
A new professional in Japan had a capped salary for years, and a typical transfer fee to Europe was small. Europe paid more and offered a bigger stage.
Japanese players in major European leagues rose about 90% in five years, according to Nikkei Asia.
The J.League's own study: a player leaves Japan for about ¥100 million, plays in a mid-level European league, and is then sold for about ¥2 billion. The second club keeps that profit.

sections.title: How agents and clubs find players in Japan

rows: The old way: trips and lists. Kroth watched the J.League in person two or three times a year, kept a list, and met each player's Japanese agent face to face. He also employed a scout in Japan.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/72063?page=4
An age filter. He looked at players of about 24 or younger and called 21–22 ideal.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/56686
A trusted insider. A coach or former player who knows both countries recommends someone, as the Nagoya coach did with Honda.
https://www.vi.nl/nieuws/hoe-vvv-kennismaakte-met-een-onvergetelijk-japans-fenomeen
Player to player. Honda introduced his agent to Yoshida; Yoshida later advised Minamino and Sugawara about Southampton.
https://www.southamptonfc.com/en/news/article/sugawara-inspired-by-legend-yoshida
Today: video first. Scouts filter players on data platforms, then travel to confirm.
https://www.hudl.com/blog/japan-pathways-europe-wyscout
Younger and younger. European scouts now contact players in the under-15 to under-17 age groups and invite them to academies.
https://note.hudl.jp/n/n49272b21187e?hl=en&gs=8fe2d7305c2e
A Japanese agent inside a European agency. The German agency Sports360 has a Japanese agent based in Cologne.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/864629
A club with its own Japan network: Sint-Truiden, and Fortuna Düsseldorf's Japan desk.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/270242
The league itself. The J.League opened a London office in January 2025 to build contacts with European clubs and support transfers.
https://www.goal.com/jp/%E3%83%8B%E3%83%A5%E3%83%BC%E3%82%B9/jleague-europe-release-20241212/blt96ada6636826d7a8

cells: Yasuhiko Okudera joined 1. FC Köln in 1977 through a friendship between the Japan coach and Köln's coach. Kazuyoshi Miura went to Genoa in 1994. Hidetoshi Nakata went to Perugia in 1998, managed by a PR company.
Nobuaki Tanabe passed the FIFA exam in 1999; his company signed Junichi Inamoto, who joined Arsenal in 2001 as the first Japanese player in the Premier League.
German agent Thomas Kroth took Takahara to Hamburg, then Hasebe, Kagawa and Uchida. Kagawa cost Dortmund about €350,000 in 2010 and every German club began looking at Japan.
VVV-Venlo in the Netherlands took Honda, Yoshida and Otsu. Sint-Truiden in Belgium, Japanese-owned since 2017, took Tomiyasu, Endo and Kamada.
About 114 Japanese players were at European clubs at the start of a recent season (an NHK figure). Clubs scout Japan directly, and some players go straight from high school to Europe.

rows: A rule change at home made the wave possible: in 2009 Japan stopped clubs charging a fee for players whose contracts had ended.
https://goetheweb.jp/person/article/20240528-fujita-2
In August 2026 there were ten Japanese players at Premier League clubs, a record.
https://www.freemalaysiatoday.com/category/sports/2026/08/26/high-quality-low-risk-record-number-of-japanese-in-premier-league

parts.heading: How big is the business?
rows: OFFICIAL: clubs worldwide paid agents 1.37 billion US dollars in 2025, according to FIFA.
https://inside.fifa.com/en/news/club-agent-service-fees-reach-new-heights-2025
OFFICIAL: German clubs paid agents €297 million in 2024/25, according to the German league.
https://www.heidelberg24.de/sport/fussball/millionenregen-fuer-berater-fc-bayern-laesst-bvb-und-leipzig-alt-aussehen-zr-94327065.html
REPORTED: in Japan in 2019, players paid agents about ¥1.14 billion and J.League clubs about ¥620 million.
https://victorysportsnews.com/articles/8053

parts.heading: Why Japanese clubs often got little
rows: Short contracts. If a contract has ended, no fee is due. Many early stars left for nothing or for small compensation.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/?p=39685
Thin contracts. A J.League standard contract is about 3 pages; a Premier League one is roughly 100.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/871477
A typical release figure today is roughly ¥100–300 million (ESTIMATE from one agent). He suggests clubs add a share of any later sale.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/871478
Money does come back later. Avispa Fukuoka reportedly received over ¥100 million from Tomiyasu's later moves through solidarity payments (ESTIMATE).
https://spaia.jp/column/soccer/ws/19254
The J.League earned about ¥4.5 billion from overseas transfers in 2024, which its chairman calls too little.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/jleague_other/2025/09/14/j_14/

sections.title: The rules, and how they keep changing

cells: FIFA licence by exam. In Japan only licensed agents, lawyers and family could negotiate.
'Intermediaries' (仲介人): no exam, anyone could register with the Japan FA. About 360 were registered in 2021.
FIFA licence and exam again. About 4,500 licences at the start; 10,525 by December 2025.
20 multiple-choice questions, 75% to pass. 52% passed the first sitting in April 2023; about 40% passed in 2024.
For the player's agent: 5% of pay up to 200,000 US dollars a year, 3% above.
After a German court order, FIFA suspended the fee limits worldwide. Licensing stayed.

The EU's top court ruled. FIFA says its key rules can be justified; lawyers say the court was cautious and national courts still have to decide. FIFA plans talks before a new transfer system on 1 January 2027.

rows: 'Interest' is not an offer. Maya Yoshida says a reported interest often means the player is the third or fourth choice.
https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240
Some agents invent interest to keep a player calm when there are no offers, Yoshida warns.
https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240/p2
Fraud in lower leagues: agents take a fee and go silent, or deliver a club far below what was promised. Reported most in Germany and Southeast Asia.
https://victorysportsnews.com/articles/8053
Players share the risk. The players' union tells players to check an agent's registration, because a player can be punished together with a rule-breaking agent.
https://www.j-pfa.or.jp/intermediary/
Abroad is not automatically a step up. Shinji Okazaki says a move from Japan's second division to Germany's fifth tier is a step down, and that promises can break when a sporting director changes.
https://www.synchronous.jp/articles/-/3730
Under-18s: international transfers of minors are generally banned. Barcelona was punished and Takefusa Kubo had to return to Japan.
https://news.yahoo.co.jp/expert/articles/5bea8661ec9099616563a465240e6d1f6314d2e2
Running down a contract has a cost. Daichi Kamada's exit from Lazio in 2024 became a public row over what his agent asked for.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/?p=583385
The ad side is a separate risk. An agent negotiates with clubs; a management office accepts sponsor deals. See the Vera&John deep dive on Maya Yoshida's page.
Maya Yoshida (Dec 2025): choosing a wife and choosing an agent are the two decisions a player must not get wrong. The final decision on a move should be the player's own.
https://qoly.jp/q1/17813172
Maya Yoshida (Aug 2026): he nearly moved to China and the Middle East several times, and chose not to.
https://qoly.jp/q1/17857240/p2
Shinji Okazaki (May 2026): players who expect everything to be arranged for them struggle abroad.
https://www.synchronous.jp/articles/-/3730
Wataru Endo (2024): English clubs now rate Japanese players more highly than before.
https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/sport/archives/2024/09/18/2003823958
Agent Nobuaki Tanabe: negotiating takes one or two days a year; the rest of the job is helping the player get better.
https://plus.tver.jp/news/80698/detail/

sections.title: What comes next: 2026 and after
sections.intro: These are changes already decided or trends that sources describe. They are not my predictions.

cells: The J.League moved its season to match Europe (from August 2026)
The season now starts in August and ends in May. Japanese clubs can sell in summer, when European clubs have the most money, instead of losing players mid-season.
Fees should rise, but not by much
Sint-Truiden's chief says fees will go up a little, not double or triple, and that free transfers will also increase. It depends on each club's skill.
Salary caps for new professionals ended in February 2026 and minimum salaries began. Agents advise clubs to add a share of future sales.
More moves at 18 or straight from high school. Some in Japan worry the J.League will be hollowed out.
More direct moves to the top
Some players now skip the small-league step. Five of the 14 Japanese players in the Bundesliga in 2025/26 came straight from the J.League.
Players are coming back from Europe (Takuma Asano and Takumu Kawamura to Hiroshima), and foreign players with European records are joining the J.League.
Large agencies compete for Japanese players, some charging the player nothing.
FIFA plans talks with agents before a new transfer system on 1 January 2027. Whether fee limits return is undecided.
The players' union under Maya Yoshida is pushing for players to manage their own image rights.

sections.title: A checklist for reading any player's story (my analysis)

rows: Who vouched for the player to the first foreign club? An agent, a coach, a chairman, a teammate?
Was the first club a gateway or a destination?
Was a fee paid, or did the contract run out? Who decided that?
Did the agent change as the player rose? Why?
Who handles the ads, and is that a different company?
What did the player learn the hard way, and what do they now tell younger players?
